title: 12. Cloud, Containers & Deployment: Auto Scaling
summary: Auto scaling is the cloud capability that automatically adjusts the number of compute instances (horizontal) or the size of instances (vertical) in response to load signals, so that an application meets its demand curve…
objectives: What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling, and when do you choose each?
How does target tracking differ from step scaling?
What is predictive scaling and when is it useful?
What is the role of cooldowns and warmup in auto scaling?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Auto scaling is the cloud capability that automatically adjusts the number of compute instances (horizontal) or the size of instances (vertical) in response to load signals, so that an application meets its demand curve without over-provisioning idle capacity or under-provisioning during peaks.
Auto scaling answers a fundamental economic problem: real workload demand is not flat, but infrastructure is sold in fixed units. A typical web service sees 3–5× more traffic at peak than at trough; a retail service sees 50–100× on Black Friday versus a quiet Tuesday; a video game launch sees 0 to 1 million concurrent players in hours. Without auto scaling, you must provision for peak, which means most of your fleet sits idle (and billed) 90% of the time. With auto scaling, the fleet grows to meet demand and shrinks when demand falls, paying only for what you use. Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling Groups launched in 2009 and made this pattern mainstream; Kubernetes later added Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA), Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA), and Cluster Autoscaler (CA); and predictive scaling (using ML on historical load) has become the third generation, available on AWS since 2022. Netflix, Amazon, and every major cloud consumer treat auto scaling as a first-class architectural concern.

The first concept is horizontal versus vertical scaling. Horizontal scaling (scaling out) adds more instances of the same size — going from 10 EC2 instances to 50. Vertical scaling (scaling up) makes each instance bigger — going from m5.large to m5.2xlarge. Horizontal scaling is generally preferred because it has no upper bound (you can always add another node), it does not cause downtime (new instances join the pool while old ones keep serving), and it composes naturally with stateless architectures. Vertical scaling has an upper bound (the largest instance the cloud offers), it causes a brief interruption during resize (the instance must stop and restart under a new type), and it does not improve redundancy. But vertical scaling is simpler — no load balancer needed, no shared state problem — and it is the right answer for stateful workloads like a single MySQL primary. Auto scaling groups in the cloud support both: EC2 ASG does horizontal by default; RDS and Aurora support vertical scaling via instance class changes; Kubernetes HPA does horizontal while VPA does vertical on Pod resource requests.

The second concept is the scaling signal. A scaling policy needs a metric that correlates with the load the system can handle. The classic signal is average CPU utilization — "scale out when CPU > 70%, scale in when CPU < 30%". This works well for CPU-bound workloads but is misleading for I/O-bound or memory-bound ones. Better signals are often custom: requests per second per instance, queue depth (SQS `ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible`), latency (p99 above a threshold), or connection count. AWS Application Auto Scaling supports target tracking on many standard and custom metrics: you say "keep average CPU at 50%" and the platform calculates the scaling adjustment. Step scaling adds granularity: small adjustments for small breaches, large adjustments for large breaches. The art is choosing a metric that leads demand — a queue depth metric scales ahead of latency degradation, while a latency metric scales after users have already felt pain. Netflix uses a custom "performance index" combining CPU, latency, and error rate to drive scaling for its streaming fleet.

The third concept is target tracking versus step scaling versus simple scaling. Simple scaling waits for a breach, scales by a fixed amount, then enters a cooldown (default 300 seconds) before scaling again — slow but predictable. Step scaling scales by different amounts based on how far the metric breaches the threshold (e.g., +1 instance if CPU is 70–80%, +3 instances if 80–90%, +5 if above 90%), which responds faster to large spikes. Target tracking treats the metric as a setpoint: "keep CPU at 50%" and the platform computes the capacity needed to hold it, scaling in or out as required — this is the most common modern pattern because it requires only the target value, not the step sizes, and it naturally handles both scale-out and scale-in. Predictive scaling, the newest pattern, uses ML models trained on historical traffic to scale out *before* demand arrives — useful for predictable workloads like daily traffic peaks and event-driven launches. Amazon Prime Day combines predictive scaling (pre-warming ahead of the event) with target tracking (fine-tuning during the event) to handle the 10× traffic spike without latency degradation.

The fourth concept is cooldowns and stability. Naive auto scaling flaps: a brief CPU spike scales out, the new capacity causes CPU to drop, the policy scales in, the next spike finds the system under-provisioned again. To prevent this, every scaling policy has a cooldown — a quiet period (typically 60–300 seconds) after a scaling action during which no further scale-in can occur. Step and target tracking also use a "warmup" parameter that tells the platform how long a newly added instance takes to start serving traffic, so the metric aggregator does not consider the new instance underutilized while it is still booting. The trade-off is responsiveness versus stability: shorter cooldowns react faster but flap more; longer cooldowns are stable but lag peaks. Netflix tunes these per workload: 60-second cooldowns for stateless frontends that boot in 30 seconds, 600-second cooldowns for stateful Cassandra nodes that take minutes to join the ring.

The fifth concept is the difference between instance-level scaling (EC2 ASG, VMSS) and Pod-level scaling (Kubernetes HPA). EC2 ASG scales the number of VMs in a fleet, and each VM typically runs one application instance or a small set of containers. HPA scales the number of Pod replicas within an existing node fleet, which is faster because Pods start in milliseconds and do not require VM provisioning. In a Kubernetes cluster, you typically run both: HPA scales Pod replicas to absorb the request spike within seconds, while the Cluster Autoscaler scales nodes to provide capacity when Pods go Pending — a two-tier scaling system. This two-tier model is what makes Kubernetes feel responsive: HPA handles short-term spikes by packing more Pods onto existing nodes; CA handles sustained growth by adding nodes; and the cloud's ASG handles the actual VM provisioning. Each tier has its own cooldown and metric, so tuning them to work together without fighting is a real operational concern.

The sixth concept is the economics. Auto scaling's value proposition is that you pay for average load rather than peak load. If your peak is 5× average, auto scaling saves roughly 80% of the peak-provisioned cost — but only if the platform scales in aggressively when load drops. Many teams scale out eagerly but scale in timidly because scale-in is where mistakes happen (you can accidentally remove a node that is serving traffic, or remove too many and trigger a cascade). The conservative pattern is to scale in by smaller steps than scale-out, to use longer cooldowns for scale-in, and to use instance termination protection on stateful nodes. Spot instances amplify the savings: a fleet that is 70% on-demand baseline and 30% spot burst capacity costs roughly 60% of an all-on-demand fleet, and the spot tier can be replaced automatically by on-demand if the spot market dries up. Amazon's Prime Day fleet uses exactly this pattern, with predictive scaling to pre-warm and spot for the burst tier. The trade-off summary: auto scaling reduces cost and improves resilience, at the cost of operational complexity (metric tuning, cooldown tuning, multi-tier coordination) and the risk of cascading failures when scaling logic is wrong.

### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD Metrics[CloudWatch / Prometheus
CPU, RPS, queue depth, latency] Metrics -->|sample every 60s| TG[Target Tracking
keep CPU at 50%] Metrics -->|breach bands| SS[Step Scaling
+1 / +3 / +5 by severity] History[Historical load 14d] --> PS[Predictive Scaling
forecast demand] TG --> Decider SS --> Decider PS --> Decider Decider{Scaling Decision} Decider -->|scale out| ASGOut[ASG: capacity 10 -> 20] Decider -->|scale in| ASGIn[ASG: capacity 20 -> 12] Decider -->|no change| Hold[Hold] ASGOut --> LB[Register with Load Balancer] ASGIn --> Drain[Drain + Deregister + Terminate] Drain --> Cooldown[Cooldown 300s] Cooldown -.->|block further scale-in| Decider HPA[K8s HPA: replicas 5 -> 30] -.->|within existing nodes| Pods CA[Cluster Autoscaler: nodes 4 -> 8] -.->|when Pods Pending| ASGOut ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +-------------------+ +-----------------+ traffic ----->| Load Balancer |------->| Target Group | +---------+---------+ +--------+--------+ | | v v +---------+---------+ +--------+--------+ | Auto Scaling Grp| | fleet of EC2 | | min=4 max=50 |<------>| i-aaa (warm) | | desired=12 | | i-bbb (warm) | +---------+--------+ | i-ccc (warm) | ^ | i-ddd (booting)| | +-----------------+ +-----------------------+----------+ | Scaling Policies | | | | target-tracking: CPU -> 50% | | step: CPU 70-80% -> +1 | | CPU 80-90% -> +3 | | CPU >90% -> +5 | | predictive: forecast from 14d hist | | | | cooldown: 300s after scale-in | | warmup: 120s for new instance | +------------------------------------+ Two-tier K8s scaling: HPA: replicas 5 -> 30 within seconds (Pods start in ms) | v Pods Pending CA: nodes 4 -> 8 (provision VMs, 60-180s) | v ASG: capacity 4 -> 8 (cloud API) ``` ### Walkthrough 1. Cloud metrics (CPU, RPS, queue depth, latency, custom CloudWatch or Prometheus metrics) are sampled at a fixed interval, typically every 60 seconds, and fed into one or more scaling policies attached to an Auto Scaling Group. 2. A target-tracking policy computes the capacity adjustment needed to hold the metric at its target (e.g., 50% CPU); a step policy maps breach severity to a scaling step; a predictive policy uses historical data to pre-scale before forecasted demand arrives. 3. On a scale-out decision, the ASG launches new instances (60–180s for EC2, ms for K8s Pods), which register with the load balancer after passing health checks and a configurable warmup period. 4. On a scale-in decision, the ASG picks an instance (often the oldest or one in an AZ with the most surplus), drains it from the load balancer, terminates it, and enters a cooldown to prevent flapping.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- EC2 ASG / VMSS / K8s CA equivalent.
- Keep metric at target_value by computing required capacity.
- Adjust by step sizes based on breach severity.
- Forecast demand from history, pre-scale before peak.
- Auto_scaler.py - runnable mock of a cloud auto-scaler.
- Models: target tracking, step scaling, predictive scaling,
- Cooldowns, warmup, health checks, and two-tier K8s HPA + CA.
- Oldest-first termination for stability

**Defines:** `Instance`, `AutoScalingGroup`, `TargetTrackingPolicy`, `StepScalingPolicy`, `PredictiveScaler`

```python
# auto_scaler.py - runnable mock of a cloud auto-scaler.
# Models: target tracking, step scaling, predictive scaling,
# cooldowns, warmup, health checks, and two-tier K8s HPA + CA.
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import List, Callable, Optional
import time, math, random

@dataclass
class Instance:
    iid: str
    launched_at: float
    state: str = "warming"      # warming -> healthy -> draining -> terminated
    cpu_load: float = 0.0
    is_spot: bool = False

    def age(self, now: float) -> float:
        return now - self.launched_at

class AutoScalingGroup:
    """EC2 ASG / VMSS / K8s CA equivalent."""
    def __init__(self, name: str, min_size: int, max_size: int,
                 warmup_s: float = 120.0, cooldown_s: float = 300.0):
        self.name = name
        self.min_size = min_size
        self.max_size = max_size
        self.desired = min_size
        self.warmup_s = warmup_s
        self.cooldown_s = cooldown_s
        self.instances: List[Instance] = []
        self.last_scale_at = 0.0
        self.history: List[dict] = []

    def _now(self):
        return time.time()

    def _boot(self, n: int, now: float):
        for _ in range(n):
            iid = f"i-{random.randint(10000,99999)}"
            self.instances.append(Instance(iid, now))

    def _terminate(self, n: int, now: float):
        # Oldest-first termination for stability
        for _ in range(n):
            if not self.instances:
                break
            inst = sorted(self.instances, key=lambda x: x.launched_at)[0]
            inst.state = "draining"
            self.instances.remove(inst)

    def set_desired(self, new_desired: int, reason: str):
        now = self._now()
        new_desired = max(self.min_size, min(self.max_size, new_desired))
        if new_desired == self.desired:
            return
        delta = new_desired - self.desired
        if delta > 0:
            self._boot(delta, now)
            print(f"[asg:{self.name}] scale-out +{delta} "
                  f"({self.desired}->{new_desired}) reason={reason}")
        else:
            # scale-in respects cooldown
            if now - self.last_scale_at < self.cooldown_s:
                print(f"[asg:{self.name}] scale-in blocked by cooldown "
                      f"({int(self.cooldown_s - (now - self.last_scale_at))}s left)")
                return
            self._terminate(-delta, now)
            print(f"[asg:{self.name}] scale-in {delta} "
                  f"({self.desired}->{new_desired}) reason={reason}")
        self.desired = new_desired
        self.last_scale_at = now
        self.history.append({"t": now, "desired": new_desired, "reason": reason})

    def active_capacity(self, now: float) -> int:
        # Only healthy (past warmup) instances count for capacity
        return sum(1 for i in self.instances
                   if i.state != "terminated" and i.age(now) >= self.warmup_s)

    def avg_cpu(self, now: float) -> float:
        active = [i for i in self.instances
                  if i.state != "terminated" and i.age(now) >= self.warmup_s]
        if not active:
            return 0.0
        return sum(i.cpu_load for i in active) / len(active)

class TargetTrackingPolicy:
    """Keep metric at target_value by computing required capacity."""
    def __init__(self, metric_fn: Callable[[], float], target: float):
        self.metric_fn = metric_fn
        self.target = target

    def compute_desired(self, current_capacity: int) -> tuple:
        metric = self.metric_fn()
        if current_capacity == 0:
            return 1, f"metric={metric:.1f} (cold start)"
        # required = current * (metric / target), with small breach band
        ratio = metric / self.target
        if 0.9 <= ratio <= 1.1:
            return current_capacity, f"metric={metric:.1f} within band"
        new_cap = max(1, math.ceil(current_capacity * ratio))
        return new_cap, f"metric={metric:.1f} target={self.target} -> cap={new_cap}"

class StepScalingPolicy:
    """Adjust by step sizes based on breach severity."""
    def __init__(self, metric_fn: Callable[[], float], threshold: float,
                 steps: List[tuple]):
        # steps: list of (upper_bound, adjustment)
        self.metric_fn = metric_fn
        self.threshold = threshold
        self.steps = steps

    def compute_adjustment(self) -> tuple:
        metric = self.metric_fn()
        breach = metric - self.threshold
        if breach <= 0:
            return -1, f"metric={metric:.1f} below threshold, scale-in -1"
        for upper, adj in self.steps:
            if breach <= upper:
                return adj, f"metric={metric:.1f} breach={breach:.1f} -> {adj:+d}"
        return self.steps[-1][1], f"metric={metric:.1f} breach={breach:.1f} -> {self.steps[-1][1]:+d}"

class PredictiveScaler:
    """Forecast demand from history, pre-scale before peak."""
    def __init__(self, history_pattern: Callable[[float], float]):
        # history_pattern: returns expected load factor at time-of-day
        self.pattern = history_pattern

    def forecast(self, now: float) -> float:
        return self.pattern(now)

# ---- demo ----
if __name__ == "__main__":
    asg = AutoScalingGroup("web-asg", min_size=4, max_size=50,
                           warmup_s=2.0, cooldown_s=5.0)  # short for demo
    asg._boot(4, time.time())
    target = TargetTrackingPolicy(lambda: asg.avg_cpu(time.time()), target=50.0)

    # Simulate a traffic spike over 30 ticks (each tick = 1 second)
    traffic_curve = [30, 35, 60, 80, 95, 90, 70, 55, 45, 40,
                     35, 30, 25, 60, 85, 90, 70, 50, 40, 35]
    print("tick  cpu   desired  active  reason")
    for tick, load in enumerate(traffic_curve):
        now = time.time()
        # Assign load across active instances (warm ones share the burden)
        active = [i for i in asg.instances
                  if i.state != "terminated" and i.age(now) >= asg.warmup_s]
        if active:
            per_inst = load * len(active) / max(1, len(active))  # avg per inst
            # Re-derive each instance's CPU from total / active count
            for i in active:
                i.cpu_load = load  # simplified: each instance carries the avg
        # Target tracking decision
        new_desired, reason = target.compute_desired(asg.desired)
        asg.set_desired(new_desired, reason)
        print(f"{tick:3d}  {load:4.0f}  {asg.desired:7d}  "
              f"{asg.active_capacity(now):6d}  {reason}")
        time.sleep(0.05)  # speed up demo

    print("\n-- final history --")
    for h in asg.history[-6:]:
        print(h)
```

quiz.question: What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling, and when do you choose each?
options: Cooldown is the quiet period after a scaling action during which the ASG will not perform another scale-in (and sometimes scale-out).
It is useful for workloads with predictable diurnal or weekly patterns — a retail site that peaks at 10am and 8pm every day, a gaming service that spikes on weekend evenings, a tax-prep…
Scale-out is forgiving — adding capacity when load is high rarely causes problems beyond cost.
Horizontal is preferred for stateless workloads because it has no upper bound (you can keep adding instances), it does not cause downtime (new nodes join the pool while old ones serve),…
quiz.explanation: Horizontal scaling (scaling out) adds more instances of the same size — 10 EC2s become 50. Vertical scaling (scaling up) makes each instance bigger — m5.large becomes m5.2xlarge.

quiz.question: How does target tracking differ from step scaling?
options: Spot instances are spare cloud capacity offered at up to 90% discount, with the caveat that the cloud can reclaim them with 2 minutes' notice.
The fundamental problem is that the ASG's metric (typically CPU) does not capture the WebSocket load.
Pods go Pending when the scheduler cannot find a node with enough allocatable CPU, memory, GPU, or other requested resources.
Target tracking lets you specify a desired value for a metric — "keep average CPU at 50%" — and the platform computes the capacity adjustment needed to hold that target.
quiz.explanation: Target tracking lets you specify a desired value for a metric — "keep average CPU at 50%" — and the platform computes the capacity adjustment needed to hold that target. If CPU is 80% with 10 instances, the platform reasons that 10 × (80/50) = 16 instances are needed and scales out to 16.

Without cooldown, the system flaps: a brief CPU spike triggers scale-out, the new instances cause CPU to drop, scale-in triggers, the next spike finds the system under-provisioned, and the cycle repeats.

quiz.question: How does Kubernetes HPA differ from the Cluster Autoscaler, and how do they compose?
options: Do not rely on reactive scaling alone — a 10× spike will overwhelm any reactive system before it scales.
Spot instances are spare cloud capacity offered at up to 90% discount, with the caveat that the cloud can reclaim them with 2 minutes' notice.
The fundamental problem is that the ASG's metric (typically CPU) does not capture the WebSocket load.
HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) scales the number of Pod replicas within the existing node fleet.
quiz.explanation: HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) scales the number of Pod replicas within the existing node fleet. It watches a metric (CPU, memory, or custom via Prometheus adapter) every 15–30 seconds and adjusts the Deployment's replica count. Pod startup is in milliseconds, so HPA responds in seconds — but only if there is node capacity to schedule the new Pods.
